Each setup included a grid simulator (providing the AC voltage source), an AC measurement unit, the inverter under test, a DC measurement unit, and a programmable DC power supply. We used a real-time digital simulator with analog input cards to synchronize and record all measurements. During the tests, the programmable DC supply output was varied to mimic different DC input power levels (stepping from 100% down to 75%, 50%, and 25%). The grid simulator supplied the AC voltage and frequency conditions for the inverter. To control the experiment, we wrote a Python script that synchronized the grid simulator with the controllable DC supply, automatically updating voltage/frequency and irradiance together. A flowchart of this automated process is illustrated in Fig. 1. Grid Simulator Experiment Start Voltage/ Frequency Updates Data Collection Stop Data Controlled DC Collection Supply Start Changes Experiment End No Scenarios ≥ Threshold Yes Figure1.Experimentflowchart (Bennai et al. 2024). 2.1 Voltage Run In the voltage-run experiments, the grid frequency was maintained at 60 Hz, while the AC voltage amplitude was varied. Specifically, we swept the reference voltage from 0.9 to 1.1 per unit (p.u.) in 0.025 p.u. steps. Both inverters were tested under the same sequence of conditions. For the three-phase inverter, we sampled all voltage and current channels at 1 kHz for about 442.2 seconds. The split-phase inverter was recorded at the same sampling rate for the same duration. The three-phase inverter line-to-neutral RMS voltages varied roughly from 247 V (0.9 p.u.) up to 304 V (1.1 p.u.). Its line current RMS ranged from about 6.7 A at the lowest voltage to about 25.7 A at the highest. In the split-phase setup (nominally 120 V per phase), the same 0.9–1.1 p.u. range corresponds to about 108 V to 132 V RMS, pro- ducing currents from roughly 7.9 A to 32.5 A. These measurements (see Tables 1 and 2) confirm that both inverters produced smoothly increasing output currents as the AC voltage was raised. This dataset of voltages and currents at various voltage levels provides one portion of our training data for the ML models. More information on the inverters and data collection can be found in Ref. (Bennai et al. 2024). 2.2 Frequency Run In the frequency-run experiments, we fixed the AC voltage amplitude at 1.0 p.u. and stepped the grid frequency through a set of values: 59.4 Hz, 59.6 Hz, 59.8 Hz, 60.2 Hz, 60.4 Hz, and 60.45 Hz. Again, both inverters were tested in this sequence. The three-phase inverter data were recorded at 1 kHz for about 247.65 seconds, and the split-phase data for about 247.97 seconds. To analyze the effect of these frequency changes, we applied a short- time Fourier transform (STFT) to the recorded Phase A voltage and current, allowing the signal’s spectral content to evolve with the stepped frequency changes.
